cells.tense: You are standing where something finishes and your weight is already on the next step.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're letting end on purpose, and tell one person this week — as a decision, not a complaint.
cells.core:
Something is being cleared and you have a hand in it. Most endings arrive and nobody signs for them; here you put something down on purpose, without waiting for permission about the timing. That is the healthy version of this — a direction picked, and the picking not relitigated every morning.

What steadies it is grip that holds without crushing. You keep pressure on while the thing actually finishes, instead of slamming the door to be done with it or holding the frame so nothing can close. A week like this is quieter than a clean break and heavier than giving up. Mostly the work is staying in the room while it ends.
cells.sheetLine: You're choosing what ends, and you're the one who picked it.
cells.place: at the edge of something that has to end

cells.tense: You are bracing for a finished version of this that nobody has promised you yet.
cells.ask: Set a time to stop working on it today, do the last thing, and leave it alone until morning.
cells.core:
The ending hasn't finished on its own and you've stepped in to finish it yourself — steering talks toward the conclusion, reading slow days as failure, rehearsing the calm you'll feel when it's over. The calm is being spent in advance.

What's actually running is fear of the middle, where an ending is still moving and can't be managed. So you take the wheel early and decide how it should go, when it should be done, and who should be fine about it first. It's the same drive to choose, pushed past the point where choosing helps — and the people in it can feel the push.
cells.sheetLine: You're pushing an ending instead of letting it complete.

cells.tense: You are still waiting outside a door that already closed behind you.
cells.ask: Pick one small thing that has nothing to do with the ending, and carry it all the way through today.
cells.core:
Something finished and no direction replaced it. Choosing runs on a certain current, and yours is running somewhere else — so days go by on what's left over, and starting anything feels like a bill you can't pay.

This isn't laziness and it isn't a lack of feeling. It's a starved part of you: the one that points at one thing and says 'this, not that' hasn't been fed since the last thing ended. So you wait for a sign, or for someone else to decide, or for the morning you wake up wanting something. That morning isn't scheduled.

What would feed it isn't another ending. It's one small direction, picked today, kept whether or not it feels like much.
cells.sheetLine: You're waiting for direction to arrive instead of picking one.

cells.tense: You are directing what stays and what goes, and calling it the way things turned out.
cells.ask: Take one thing you've been treating as already decided, and say to yourself it was your call.
cells.core:
Look at what you've let go of and what you've kept. Which messages get answered, who still gets your time, which version of events you tell. That's direction, and it's been running the whole time without your name on it.

It wears the costume of circumstance. You weren't choosing, you were busy, it just worked out that way. But someone sorted it — kept this, dropped that, stopped reaching out here. That someone is the one reading this.

No announcement is required. Just one moment where the choice steps out from behind the story of how things went and stands there as yours, and you let it.
cells.sheetLine: You're the one sorting what stays. You've been calling it life.

attempts.check: The record says 'you know it' at Balanced, but the kernel gives no evidence the person is conscious of their own authorship, so that would be my embellishment, not theirs. A reader could reasonably say they don't feel like they're choosing anything — they're just getting through the goodbye. The ask survives either way: if my read is wrong, telling one person that a change is the person's call still costs nothing and teaches them where their authorship sits. The sentence that serves me more than them would be any line about 'knowing what you're doing' — it flatters the reading instead of giving them something to use.
